ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in the rhombus $ABCD$, the perpendicular bisector of $AD$ intersects $AD$ at point $E$, and intersects $AC$ at point $F$, $\angle ABC=4\angle DFC$, what is the measure of $\angle BAD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} As shown in the diagram,\\
$\because EF$ perpendicularly bisects $AD$.\\
$\therefore AF=DF$.\\
$\therefore \angle FAD=\angle FDA$.\\
$\because \angle DFC=\angle FAD+\angle FDA$.\\
$\therefore \angle FDC=2\angle FAD$.\\
In rhombus $ABCD$, $AC$ is the diagonal,\\
$\therefore \angle BAD=2\angle FAD$.\\
$\therefore \angle BAD=\angle DFC$.\\
$\because \angle ABC=4\angle DFC$.\\
$\therefore \angle ABC=4\angle BAD$.\\
$\because \angle BAD+\angle ABC=180^\circ$.\\
$\therefore \angle BAD+4\angle BAD=180^\circ$.\\
$\therefore \angle BAD=\boxed{36^\circ}$

method.method_draft: Coordinate/vector route. Read the diagram as the rhombus A-D-C-B with diagonal AC drawn; use the text to define F as the intersection of AC with the perpendicular bisector of AD. Let x = ∠BAD. Put A = (0,0), B = (1,0), D = (cos x, sin x), so C = (1 + cos x, sin x). Then ∠ABC = 180° - x. Since F lies on AC, write F = tC = t(1 + cos x, sin x). Since F lies on the perpendicular bisector of AD and AD has length 1, F satisfies F · D = 1/2. Thus t[(1 + cos x)cos x + sin^2 x] = 1/2, so t(1 + cos x) = 1/2. Hence F = (1/2, sin x/[2(1 + cos x)]) = (1/2, (1/2)tan(x/2)). The direction of AC, and therefore FC, makes angle x/2 with AB. Computing the slope of FD from F to D gives tan(3x/2), so FD makes direction angle 3x/2. Therefore ∠DFC = 3x/2 - x/2 = x. Now the given condition becomes 180° - x = 4x, yielding x = 36°. Thus ∠BAD = 36°.

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, in the rhombus $ABCD$, the perpendicular bisector of $AD$ intersects $AD$ at point $E$, and intersects $AC$ at point $F$. If $\angle ABC=4\angle DFC$, what is the measure of $\angle BAD$?
raw_record.answer:
Solution: As shown in the diagram,
$\because EF$ perpendicularly bisects $AD$.
$\therefore AF=DF$.
$\therefore \angle FAD=\angle FDA$.
$\because \angle DFC=\angle FAD+\angle FDA$.
$\therefore \angle DFC=2\angle FAD$.
In rhombus $ABCD$, $AC$ is the diagonal,
$\therefore \angle BAD=2\angle FAD$.
$\therefore \angle BAD=\angle DFC$.
$\because \angle ABC=4\angle DFC$.
$\therefore \angle ABC=4\angle BAD$.
$\because \angle BAD+\angle ABC=180^\circ$.
$\therefore \angle BAD+4\angle BAD=180^\circ$.
$\therefore \angle BAD=\boxed{36^\circ}$
raw_record.final_cot:
First describe the image: In the figure, a rhombus-shaped quadrilateral ABCD can be seen, vertex A is on the left, C is on the right, D is above, B is below, the order of vertices is A-D-C-B, and the diagonal AC from A to C is drawn. In the small figure, E, F, and the perpendicular bisector are not clear or not obviously marked, so determine according to the problem statement: E is on AD, F is on AC, and EF is the perpendicular bisector of AD.
Then reason: Let x=∠BAD, let y=∠FAD. Because ABCD is a rhombus, the diagonal AC of the rhombus bisects ∠BAD; and F is on AC, so y=∠FAD=x/2. Because F is on the perpendicular bisector of AD, AF=DF, therefore △ADF is an isosceles triangle, ∠FAD=∠FDA=y. Because A, F, C are collinear, ∠DFC is the exterior angle of △ADF at F, so ∠DFC=∠FAD+∠FDA=2y=x. Adjacent interior angles of a rhombus are supplementary, so ∠ABC=180°−x. The problem gives ∠ABC=4∠DFC, therefore 180°−x=4x, solving gives 5x=180°, x=36°. So ∠BAD=36°.
